title: Inner humility (III.5–III.6)
hookLine: your name is called, every face turns, and out comes "oh, it was nothing"; Francis de Sales doesn't trust that answer
tomorrow: what if your anger is fair? why does Francis still shut the door?

lines: YOUR NAME, AND EVERY FACE TURNS.
cards: The gym is full. Someone at the microphone reads out a name, and it's yours. Every face turns.
You walk up, take the certificate, someone says great job, and out it comes before you can stop it: oh, it was nothing. It sounds humble. It comes out almost by reflex.
Francis de Sales, writing to Philothea, the reader of his book, doesn't quite trust that answer. What he thinks is going on under it is a little uncomfortable.

teach.b: Here's what he sees. First, look at the gift. Some people, Francis says, won't let themselves think about the good God has given them, for fear of pride.
That's a mistake. Seeing a gift clearly, and seeing whose it is, leads to thanks and to love of the giver, not to vanity. Second, the words.
We often call ourselves nothing, he says, misery itself, and we'd be stung if anyone took us at our word. Third, the motive.

That kind of lowering, he says, can be a way of running off so that someone will chase us. Say it was nothing, and wait for someone to insist it was something. So the answer in the gym may be less humble than it sounds.
Real humility, as he describes it, doesn't make a show or pile up humble words. It doesn't turn down a good task out of pretended modesty.
Fourth, in the next chapter, he uses an old word, abjection, for our lowliness, and says the humble person comes to love it: being plain, or weak, or overlooked, or caught in a small clumsy moment.
Not their faults, he's careful to say.
Their smallness, carried gently, without fuss and without hiding it.
Inner humility lets the truth be the truth, about the gift and about the smallness both. Sometimes the most honest answer is the shortest one.

how: Catholics count humility as a foundation of the spiritual life; some pray the Litany of Humility, and some bring both their gifts and their failings to prayer and to confession.

o: humility in the heart: honest about gifts and smallness
a private vow never to accept any praise at all
the habit of always putting others' needs before your own

p: would sting if taken at our word
running off so someone will chase

s: humility, for Francis, means believing you have nothing good in you
he says to look at your gifts clearly, see they're God's, and give thanks.
he warns that calling ourselves nothing can be a way of fishing for praise
running off so that someone will chase us.
Francis says the humble person learns to love their own faults
not their faults: their smallness and lowliness, carried gently.

games.q: your younger sister made the honor roll and keeps saying "i'm so dumb though" at dinner. what would Francis's humility say to her?
o: see the gift clearly, be thankful for it, and drop the act.
keep talking herself down so she doesn't get proud.
tell everyone her grades so they know she's smart.
games.why: Francis says looking at a gift and seeing whose it is leads to thanks; calling yourself nothing can be a way of being chased.

practice: Bring back one real compliment you've been given, recent or old. Through the sit, let it be true without arguing with it, and then say, quietly, out loud: thank you. If you pray, thank God for the gift underneath it.

wordCard.voice: Inner humility. Humility in the heart, where only God sees it: honest about the gifts and about the smallness both.

carryVoice: Your line: true humility, the kind that can just say thank you. See you tomorrow.
